passage:
I'm Sudha, and I've been at the newsroom of a Pune paper for a year. The thing I'll remember is one Tuesday meeting.
Gargi, our editor, walked in and said, "Before anything else: yesterday's flood headline was my call, and it was wrong. The numbers were from the old report. I've sent the correction." Nobody had to hunt for a culprit.
Then she said Rohit's photo had carried the whole front page, and asked me, the most junior person there, what readers in my area were talking about. I stammered through something about water tankers. She wrote it on the board.
My old boss at a magazine had a bigger title and a louder voice, and we did what he said because we had to. With Gargi, people stay late because they want to. I didn't understand the difference until I watched it.

qa.q: What did Gargi say was wrong with the flood headline?
qa.a: The numbers were from the old report.

qa.q: How did Sudha feel being asked for a view in the meeting?
qa.a: Sudha felt nervous, stammering through the answer, but also valued when Gargi wrote it on the board.

qa.q: What could Sudha take from Gargi's style for the future?
qa.a: Own mistakes openly, give specific credit and ask the quietest people for their view; that builds trust a title alone cannot.

qa.q: How might Rohit feel hearing Gargi credit the photo in front of everyone?
qa.a: Rohit probably felt proud and noticed, which makes the extra effort feel worthwhile.

grounding: Shows a junior watching a leader who admits a mistake, credits others and asks for views, and learning that trust outlasts positional authority.

passage:
Tenzin,
Congratulations on the new team! You asked how I manage mine without going mad.
Honestly, I used to run everyone the same way: daily check-ins, detailed notes on everything. Leela, who's been here eight years, told me politely it felt like being watched. Kabir, who'd just joined, told me nothing at all, and was quietly drowning.
So I started asking each person one question: "What do you need from me this month?" Leela said: leave me alone, review at the end. Now she gets a Friday chat and full freedom. Kabir said he didn't know where to start, so we sit together fifteen minutes each morning and I show him how I'd break a task down. Everyone, Leela included, still gets honest feedback when something isn't working, just in different doses.
It's more work at first. It's much less work later.
Call me after your first week.
Abhinav

qa.q: How long has Leela been there?
qa.a: Eight years.

qa.q: What was Kabir feeling in the early weeks?
qa.a: Kabir felt lost and overwhelmed, "quietly drowning", but didn't say anything.

qa.q: What question did Abhinav start asking, and why does it work?
qa.a: "What do you need from me this month?"; it lets each person get the right mix of freedom and guidance instead of one habit for all.

qa.q: How did Leela experience Abhinav's old style?
qa.a: Leela felt watched and a little stifled, as if eight years of experience counted for nothing.

grounding: Shows a leader who asks each person what they need, giving freedom to the experienced, guidance to the new and honest feedback to everyone.

passage:
It was raining, so all five children were stuck in the small playroom with one tub of blocks. Akash and Tarun started a tower together.
"Red one here!" Akash said.
"No, mine goes there!" Tarun grabbed it. The tower wobbled. Akash's lip shook. Diya and Ravi watched from the corner.
Mira aunty sat down between the boys. "One block for Akash, one block for Tarun. Let's count."
Slowly they took turns. At twelve blocks the tower stood tall. Tarun clapped. Akash put the last block on top, very carefully.

qa.q: How many blocks tall was the tower when it stood tall?
qa.a: Twelve blocks.

qa.q: What does Akash's shaking lip suggest?
qa.a: Akash felt upset and frustrated when Tarun grabbed the block and the tower wobbled.

qa.q: How did Mira aunty help the boys take turns?
qa.a: She sat between them and made turns simple and fair, one block each, and counted with them.

qa.q: How might Tarun feel when the tower stands tall?
qa.a: Tarun feels proud and happy, clapping for the tower they built together.

grounding: Shows young children arguing over who places which block, with an adult helping them take turns, the seed of teamwork.

passage:
I'm Irfan. Last Friday in games period, Sir made me and Rohan captains for football. I felt like a king.
I picked the fast boys first: Sameer, then Kunal, then Ali. Soon only Yogesh was left. He's slow and wears thick glasses. I sighed loudly and said, "Fine, Yogesh." His face went red.
In the match, the other team kept scoring from long kicks. Then Yogesh said, "Put me in goal. I'm good at watching." I didn't believe him, but I let him. He saved three shots! We won 3–2.
On the way back, I told him sorry for the sigh. Next time I'll think about what each person is good at, not just who runs fastest.

qa.q: How many shots did Yogesh save?
qa.a: He saved three shots.

qa.q: Why did Irfan say sorry on the way back?
qa.a: Irfan felt guilty and a bit ashamed of the loud sigh after seeing how much Yogesh helped the team win.

qa.q: What will Irfan do differently when picking a team next time?
qa.a: Think about what each person is good at, like watching the ball in goal, not only speed.

qa.q: What was it like for Yogesh to be picked last with a sigh?
qa.a: Yogesh felt embarrassed and hurt, his face going red, before getting a chance to show his strength.

grounding: Shows children choosing sides, with the pride of picking first and the sting of being picked last, and learning a team needs different strengths.

passage:
Dear Diary,
Today at PT, team picking again. I stood on the line while names got called: Rahul, Vicky, Sam, everyone. My shoes got really interesting.
When three of us were left, I joked about being "saved for last like the best sweet". Everybody laughed. I laughed too, even though my stomach felt like a stone.
Then Joseph, captain of the blue side, said, "Anirban! I wanted you. You always pass instead of hogging." He said it like he meant it, and gave me a high five.
I passed to him twice and he scored once. At lunch he sat next to me.
Maybe I'm not bad at football. Maybe I'm just not fast.
Anirban

qa.q: What did Anirban joke about being saved for last like?
qa.a: Like the best sweet.

qa.q: How did Anirban feel while making the joke?
qa.a: Anirban felt hurt and embarrassed, stomach "like a stone", and used the joke to hide it.

qa.q: How could the PT teacher make team picking kinder?
qa.a: Make teams by counting off or drawing names, so nobody has to stand on a line waiting to be chosen.

qa.q: Why might Joseph have picked Anirban so warmly?
qa.a: Joseph seems to value passing, and may have seen how the waiting hurt, so he made Anirban feel wanted.

grounding: Shows a child left until the end of team picking who laughs it off while hurting, and a kind captain whose warm pick eases the sting.

passage:
In the robotics lab after school, the argument started over the presentation slides and soon wasn't about slides at all.
"I'm presenting," Raghav said. "I wrote the code."
"And I built the arm," Nandini said. "Last time you presented, you said 'my robot' six times."
Kiran and Tushar exchanged looks and kept soldering.
"That's not..." Raghav stopped. "Fine. You present, then."
"I don't even want to present," Nandini said, her voice cracking. "I want you to say 'we'."
The lab went quiet except for the fan. Raghav looked at the arm she'd built, the neat wiring, the tiny labels.
"Okay," he said slowly. "We split it. You do the build, I do the code. And I'll say 'we'."
Tushar let out a breath. "Great. Now can someone hold this wire?"

qa.q: How many times did Raghav say "my robot" last time?
qa.a: Six times.

qa.q: What does Nandini's voice cracking reveal?
qa.a: Nandini felt hurt and unrecognised; the fight was really about wanting her work acknowledged, not about presenting.

qa.q: What helped settle the fight?
qa.a: Nandini named the real issue, and Raghav looked at her work and agreed to share the stage and say "we".

qa.q: How did Tushar experience the argument?
qa.a: Tushar felt tense and awkward, keeping his head down, and relieved when it ended.

grounding: Shows teenagers on a team clashing over who presents, where the fight is really about credit and recognition.

passage:
The volleyball court behind the Champhai school was still muddy from rain when the girls lost the district semi-final, 21–25 in the last set. Nobody spoke on the walk to the bus. Lalremsiami, who had missed the last serve, kept her face to the window.
Vinita, the captain, stood at the front of the rattling bus. "That last set is on me. I called the wrong rotation and put Mawii out of position. We'll fix it in practice." Then she went down the aisle. "Mawii, your blocks in the first set were unreal. Lalremsiami, your serves won us the quarter-final. Tlangi, you kept us calm."
Lalremsiami looked up. "I missed the last one."
"And I put you in a bad spot to serve it," Vinita said. "We lost together."
At practice on Monday, Mawii was the first to say, "I think I'm late on my jumps. Can we work on that?"

qa.q: What was the score in the last set?
qa.a: 21–25 in the last set.

qa.q: What does Lalremsiami keeping her face to the window suggest?
qa.a: Lalremsiami felt ashamed and guilty about missing the last serve, expecting to be blamed.

qa.q: What did Vinita get right as captain?
qa.a: She took her share of the blame first, praised each player's specific part, and told Lalremsiami they lost together.

qa.q: What does Mawii's question on Monday show about how the team feels now?
qa.a: Mawii feels safe to admit a weakness, because the captain showed that mistakes can be named without shame 🙂

grounding: Shows a team captain crediting each member and taking a share of the blame after a loss, which makes mistakes safe to admit.

passage:
I'm Tarun, and I was the quietest one in our five-member design project team, so mostly I watched.
Week one, everyone was polite. Mehak said "great idea" to everything. Nobody disagreed, and we got almost nothing done.
Week three, it cracked. Mehak and Arjun argued for twenty minutes about the colour scheme, then about who was "always late". Pooja walked out once. I sat there with my stomach churning and seriously thought about asking to switch teams.
Week five, something shifted. Mehak said, "I'll take layout, Arjun takes colour, and we stop fighting about each other's parts." Arjun actually laughed. We started meeting on time.
I can't say what changed in their heads. But I'm glad I didn't leave in week three, because the team we became was better than the polite one.

qa.q: How long did Mehak and Arjun argue about the colour scheme?
qa.a: For twenty minutes.

qa.q: How did Tarun feel during week three?
qa.a: Tarun felt anxious, stomach churning, and was tempted to switch teams.

qa.q: What might Tarun tell another quiet member stuck in a week-three team?
qa.a: That early fights are normal, and teams often find a way to split the work if you stay and give it time.

qa.q: How might Mehak have experienced the change from week three to week five?
qa.a: Mehak probably felt frustrated during the fights, then relieved to find a split that let everyone own a part.

grounding: Shows a student watching a new project team move from polite to tense to workable, and staying instead of giving up.

subtype: Trust broken by a missed deadline [Receiver]
passage:
At 11 p.m. in the engineering lab, Siddharth stared at the shared folder. The data analysis Mehak had promised by Monday was still an empty file. It was Wednesday. The report was due Friday.
He had messaged on Monday night: "How's it going?" Mehak replied with a thumbs-up. Tuesday: "Need anything?" Nothing. Today she'd walked past him in the canteen, chatting with Tara and Rohit, and said nothing.
Siddharth wasn't even angry about the delay. People get sick; labs overrun. It was the thumbs-up. It meant he couldn't believe the next one.
At 11:40 Mehak finally texted: "Sorry. Totally stuck on the stats. Didn't want to admit it."
Siddharth read it twice. He typed, "We can fix stuck. I just need to know," and then, slowly, opened the file himself.

qa.q: By when had Mehak promised the data analysis?
qa.a: By Monday.

qa.q: What was Siddharth feeling about Mehak's thumbs-up?
qa.a: Siddharth felt let down and distrustful; the empty thumbs-up made any future promise from Mehak hard to believe.

qa.q: What could Mehak do differently next time she's stuck?
qa.a: Say so early, even just "I'm stuck on the stats", so the team can help before the deadline.

qa.q: Why might Mehak have stayed silent?
qa.a: Mehak was probably embarrassed and afraid of looking incapable, so hiding felt easier than admitting she was stuck.

grounding: Shows a team member let down by a teammate who missed a deadline without saying so, where the silence damages trust more than the delay.

passage:
For six weeks Sumit smiled through it. On every client call Karthik took the last slot to "add a quick point", which was always Sumit's point, said louder. Sumit said nothing. It wasn't worth a scene, he told himself. At home he complained to his flatmate; at work he typed "Sure, no problem!" in the chat.
On Thursday, in the small meeting room with Anjali and the new intern, Karthik reached over and moved Sumit's coffee mug off the laptop charger. That was all.
Sumit stood up so fast his chair hit the wall. "Can you stop touching my things and stop taking my work? Every single call!"
The intern froze. Anjali stared at the table.
Karthik blinked. "I... didn't know you felt that way."
Sumit sat down, face hot, hands shaking. The mug was not the problem. It never had been.

qa.q: What did Karthik move off the laptop charger?
qa.a: Sumit's coffee mug.

qa.q: What was Sumit feeling during the six weeks of smiling?
qa.a: Sumit felt growing irritation and resentment, hidden behind "Sure, no problem!" in the chat.

qa.q: What could Sumit have done in the first week?
qa.a: Tell Karthik privately and calmly that repeating his points on calls bothered him, before the anger built up.

qa.q: What was the outburst like for the intern?
qa.a: The intern froze, probably shocked and uncomfortable at a sudden blow-up with no idea of its history.

grounding: Shows a team member hiding irritation for weeks behind smiles until a tiny trigger sets off an outburst.
